title: Forces and Newton's Laws — Motion Needs No Cause

info.text: Forces are not properties a moving thing carries but interactions between bodies, and Newton's three laws form one system for accounting for them: motion persists without any cause, a nonzero net force produces acceleration in proportion to mass, and every push is one half of an equal and opposite pair. The lesson this board teaches: stop asking what keeps a thing moving, and ask what the net force is.

clusters.name: Motion without a cause
clusters.fact: Newton's first law: a body's velocity changes only when a net force acts on it, so motion itself needs no explanation. The slowing and stopping we see everywhere is friction and drag at work — which is why a skydiver, once drag grows to balance weight, coasts down at a constant terminal velocity.

termInfo.balanced forces: Forces that cancel exactly: their vector sum is zero, so the motion does not change. A book on a table has gravity and the table's push in balance.
termInfo.friction: The force between surfaces that opposes their sliding — the hidden stopper behind the mistaken belief that moving things need a push to keep moving.
termInfo.inertia: A body's resistance to any change in its velocity: the reason coasting things keep coasting and resting things stay put. Galileo glimpsed it; Newton made it his first law.
termInfo.inertial reference frame: A frame of reference in which the first law holds — one that is not accelerating. Newton's laws are true in these frames and only in them.
termInfo.terminal velocity: The constant speed a falling body settles at once drag has grown to balance weight: zero net force, so no more acceleration.

clusters.name: The machinery of change
clusters.fact: Newton's second law makes 'force' into bookkeeping: add every push and pull as vectors into one net force, divide by the body's mass, and the result is the acceleration. The unit this arithmetic carries — the newton — is the force that gives a one-kilogram mass an acceleration of one metre per second per second.

termInfo.acceleration: The rate of change of velocity — speeding up, slowing down, or turning. What any nonzero net force produces, in proportion to that force and in inverse proportion to the mass.
termInfo.mass: The quantity of inertia in a body: the m in F = ma, saying how hard the body's velocity is to change. Not its weight — mass is the same on the Moon.
termInfo.newton (unit): The SI unit of force, 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²: the push that gives a one-kilogram mass an acceleration of one metre per second per second — roughly the weight of a small apple.

clusters.name: Forces come in pairs
clusters.fact: Newton's third law: every force is one end of an interaction between two bodies, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. A rocket's thrust pushes exhaust backward to be pushed forward; a rifle's recoil is the paired half of the bullet's launch; the floor's normal force and a rope's tension are quiet pairs holding everyday life up.

termInfo.action–reaction pair: The two halves of one interaction: A pushes B exactly as hard and exactly oppositely as B pushes A, at the same instant — and on two different bodies.
termInfo.normal force: A surface's perpendicular push against whatever presses on it — your chair pushing up on you right now. The surface's half of the contact interaction.
termInfo.recoil: The backward jolt a launcher gets when it hurls something forward: the paired half of the projectile's launch, felt by the rifle rather than the bullet.
termInfo.tension: The pull a rope, cable, or string transmits along its length — the paired stretch between whatever it connects.
termInfo.thrust: Forward force produced by throwing mass backward: a rocket pushes exhaust out one end, and the exhaust pushes the rocket forward — a third-law pair at work.

bridges.fact: The same vector sum reads both laws: add up the forces and find zero, and velocity stays constant — 'balanced forces' is just another name for zero net force. Find anything left over and it equals mass times acceleration.
bridges.info: The one number that decides everything: the vector sum of all forces acting on a body. Zero means the first law; anything left over means the second.

bridges.fact: One diagram per body: draw an arrow for every pusher so the sum can enter F = ma — and because an action–reaction pair's two halves act on two different bodies, they can never share a diagram.
bridges.info: The bookkeeper's tool: one sketch per body, an arrow for every force acting on that body. If two arrows on the same diagram claim to be a third-law pair, a mistake has already been made — the pair's halves act on two different bodies.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts name a situation in which every force has already cancelled — so nothing about the motion will change?
lenses.explanation: Inertia is the tendency that makes such situations possible, not a situation itself; friction and mass are participants in changing motion; and net force is the very quantity that reads zero here, not a situation the zero produces.

reasons.balanced forces: The cancellation itself, stated as a condition: vector sum zero, so the motion carries on unchanged.
reasons.terminal velocity: Drag has grown to balance weight; from there the fall proceeds at constant speed.

lenses.prompt: Which two quantities combine to define the unit in which every force is measured — the newton?
lenses.explanation: The newton itself is the unit being defined, and net force is the quantity the unit measures — neither is a component of the definition, which is exactly 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

reasons.acceleration: Metres per second per second: the response a force of one newton buys per kilogram.
reasons.mass: Kilograms: one newton is the force that gives one kilogram one unit of acceleration.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts name forces that hold things up or fasten them in place while nothing moves?
lenses.explanation: Thrust and recoil belong to things in motion — exhaust expelled, projectiles launched — and the action–reaction pair names the relation between two forces rather than any one holding force.

reasons.normal force: The chair's steady upward push on you: a stationary surface's half of the contact interaction.
reasons.tension: The rope's steady pull suspending the lamp — fastening without moving.

lenses.prompt: Which single concept reads both of the first two laws at once — zero and nothing changes, anything left over and the body accelerates?
lenses.explanation: Balanced forces and acceleration each describe one side only; the net force is the quantity whose value selects which law you are reading.

reasons.net force: The vector sum itself: its zero case is the first law, its nonzero case the second.

entries.reason: The conservation arc's next lesson: these three laws describe interactions frame by frame; momentum and energy are the ledgers that survive them unchanged.
The unification payoff: this board's laws plus one inverse-square force hold the Moon in its fall — an orbit as perpetual free fall.

learningIntroduction.title: Motion needs no cause
learningIntroduction.summary: Newton's three laws as one accounting system: inertia, F = ma, and the paired pushes behind every force.

content.text:
## The question Newton flipped

Everyday experience insists that moving things stop unless something keeps pushing them. Newton's first law reverses the burden: a body's velocity changes only when a net force acts on it. Motion itself needs no cause — changes in motion do. What hides the law from common sense is friction, the force between surfaces that quietly slows everything we see. Set yourself in an inertial reference frame — one that is not accelerating — and coasting simply never ends. Inertia names this stubbornness: a quantity a body has, not a condition it needs.

## The bookkeeping

When pushes and pulls do not cancel, the leftover is the net force, and it produces acceleration in proportion: F = ma. Mass is the m — the body's inertia, measured in kilograms — and acceleration is the response. The unit of force falls straight out of that arithmetic: one newton is what it takes to push one kilogram to one metre per second per second, roughly the weight of a small apple. To put the law to work, accountants of motion draw a free-body diagram: one sketch per body, an arrow for every force acting on that body, and a sum at the end.

## Every push has a partner

The third law says every force is one end of an interaction: A pushes B exactly as hard, exactly oppositely, at the same instant. The rocket's thrust is the exhaust shoved backward; the rifle's recoil is the bullet flung forward. The floor's normal force holds you up; a rope's tension holds the lamp. Because each pair's halves act on two different bodies, the two arrows of a pair never share one free-body diagram. So stop asking what keeps a thing moving. Ask what the net force is — and which paired push every force in your answer is one half of.
